priority_actions.title: Priority actions
priority_actions.summary: 5 recommended actions: 2 high, 2 medium and 1 low priority.
priority_actions.intro_source: Recommended actions to improve your IISRI rating, ordered by severity and impact.

actions.title: Close the exposed remote desktop service
actions.action_required_source: Remove public access to the remote desktop service on legacy.example.com and place it behind the VPN.
actions.why_this_matters_source: An exposed remote access service is the most common starting point for ransomware.

actions.title: Reset Compromised Credentials
actions.action_required_source: Force password resets for the exposed accounts and enable multi-factor authentication for all users.
actions.why_this_matters_source: Exposed passwords are reused in credential-stuffing attacks against the portal and email.

actions.title: Enhance DMARC Policy to "Quarantine"
actions.action_required_source: Upgrade DMARC policy from monitoring (p=none) to quarantine (p=quarantine).
actions.why_this_matters_source: Spoofed email using the organisation domain is still delivered to recipients.

actions.title: Privacy
actions.action_required_source: Vague retention periods – the policy does not say how long customer records are kept or when they are deleted.
actions.why_this_matters_source: Unclear retention periods weaken the privacy score and customer trust.

actions.title: Publish an AI use statement
actions.action_required_source: Publish a public AI policy and describe the chat assistant in the privacy policy.
actions.why_this_matters_source: Credit decisioning is a high-risk AI use under the EU AI Act; transparency is expected.

remediation_impact.narrative_source: 18 active issues were identified (6 privacy issues, 12 vulnerability findings). Completing the recommended actions is expected to recover up to 94 points, conditional on a fresh scan.

findings.finding_type: Remote desktop service exposed to the internet
findings.rationale_source: A remote desktop service answers on a public address. Exposed remote access services are a common entry point for brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks and should sit behind a VPN or zero-trust gateway.
The server still accepts TLS 1.0, a protocol version with known weaknesses that modern clients no longer need. Attackers able to force a downgrade can weaken the protection of data in transit.
The certificate presented by the host has passed its validity date. Browsers show a warning and users may learn to click through warnings, which makes interception attacks easier.
The site does not send a Strict-Transport-Security header, so a first visit over plain HTTP can be intercepted before the redirect to HTTPS takes place.
A JavaScript library version with publicly documented cross-site scripting issues is loaded by the page. Updating the library removes the known weaknesses.
No Content-Security-Policy is set. A policy limits where scripts may load from and reduces the impact of cross-site scripting.
Legacy 3DES cipher suites are still offered during the TLS handshake. They are vulnerable to birthday-bound attacks on long-lived connections.
The DMARC record is in monitoring mode only. Spoofed email that fails authentication is still delivered, which leaves the domain open to phishing and impersonation.

findings.finding_type: Server version disclosed in HTTP headers
findings.rationale_source: The web server announces its product and version in response headers. This helps attackers pick matching exploits; the header can be suppressed.
Without the nosniff option, browsers may guess content types, which can turn an uploaded file into executable content.
A session cookie can be sent over an unencrypted connection. Setting the Secure flag keeps it on HTTPS.
The zone is not signed with DNSSEC, so resolvers cannot verify that DNS answers are authentic.

findings.title: Login form served without rate limiting
findings.description: Repeated login attempts were not slowed down.
findings.remediation: Add rate limiting or a progressive delay to the login form.

findings.title: Directory listing enabled on /assets/
findings.description: The web server lists the files of a static folder.
findings.impact: Reveals file names that may help an attacker map the application.

findings.title: API documentation publicly reachable
findings.description: Interactive API documentation is reachable without authentication.
findings.impact: Gives attackers a precise map of the endpoints.
findings.remediation: Restrict the documentation to authenticated users or internal networks.

controls.line_source: SPF: Enabled – authorised sending servers are published.
DKIM: Enabled – supports email integrity and sender authenticity.
DMARC: Enabled (none mode) – visibility into spoofing attempts is present, but failing mail is not blocked.
DNSSEC: Missing / Invalid – authenticates DNS responses and protects against DNS cache poisoning.

email_dns_controls.guidance_source: It is recommended to progressively enforce DMARC policies to reduce phishing and impersonation risks. DKIM RSA keys must be at least 2048 bits; 1024-bit keys are flagged as a LOW finding. DNSSEC should be enabled (DS record + RRSIG + valid chain of trust) to prevent DNS spoofing.

scope_and_limitations.title: a. Scope and limitations
scope_and_limitations.intro: We cannot guarantee that a domain or organization is fully quantum-safe based on the results of this assessment because:
items: Post-quantum cryptography is an evolving field. Cryptographic standards, implementations, and the understanding of quantum computing capabilities continue to develop. Future advances may affect the security of algorithms considered secure today.

This is a non-invasive, external assessment. Unless an internal CyberRank agent is deployed, the scan evaluates only externally observable services and configurations. Internal systems, private networks, and services that are not externally accessible are outside the scope of this assessment.

post_quantum_readiness.title: b. Post-quantum readiness
post_quantum_readiness.intro: A domain can only be considered fully post-quantum ready if it:
items: Supports post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms for secure connections; and
Disables legacy TLS versions (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and TLS 1.2).
post_quantum_readiness.closing: Allowing legacy TLS versions enables clients to establish connections using classical cryptographic algorithms. If an attacker can force or negotiate the use of an older protocol version (a protocol downgrade), the connection may lose the protections provided by post-quantum cryptography.

c_methodology.title: Methodology and supply-chain aggregation
c_methodology.note: Generic methodology brief; values in its diagrams are illustrative.
c_methodology.headline_source: One rating for every vendor. One risk number for your whole supply chain.
c_methodology.lead_source: CYBERRANK turns externally observable evidence about an organisation into a single severity rating, a normalised risk score, and a combined risk that includes the vendors — and the vendors' vendors — behind it.

columns_source.title: The problem
columns_source.text: Attackers reach organisations through their suppliers. Existing tools don't add up: CVSS scores single technical flaws, questionnaires rely on self-reporting, and privacy, AI and quantum exposures have no common scale at all.

columns_source.title: The approach
columns_source.text: An ISO 31000-aligned model with four explicit steps, from observed weaknesses to supply-chain risk. Every step is reproducible and every number is comparable across organisations and portfolios.

columns_source.title: The regulatory fit
columns_source.text: Built for the obligations in DORA, NIS2, the GDPR and the AI Act, and aligned with ISO/IEC 27001, 27701 and 42001, NIST SP 800-53 and 800-161, PCI DSS and the NIST CSF.

steps_source.title: Observe
steps_source.text: Continuous external signals are collected without touching the organisation's systems.
steps_source.callout: Certified controls earn credits: ISO 27001, ISO 27701, SOC 2, ISAE 3402, PCI DSS. Optional questionnaires add a second, bounded evidence channel.

steps_source.title: Rate
steps_source.text: Every organisation starts with a full point budget, split evenly between a security bucket and a privacy bucket. Weaknesses deduct capped demerits; certifications add capped credits.
steps_source.callout: The net score maps to the IISRI rating, AAA to D. The rating reflects the organisation's own posture only — a vendor's weakness never changes it.

steps_source.title: Score the risk
steps_source.text: Likelihood = threat probability × weakness. Threat probability comes from sector, size and internet exposure; weakness comes from the rating. Impact is one of four tiers you assign: Critical, High, Medium or Low.
steps_source.callout: Risk = normalised likelihood × impact, reported as a score and a band: Low, Medium, High or Critical.

steps_source.title: Combine
steps_source.text: Vendors and sub-vendors are discovered automatically and rated with the same pipeline. Their risks are folded into yours, attenuated by distance in the chain.
steps_source.callout: The combined risk shows the cascading exposure that your own rating cannot see.

c_methodology.scale_caption_source: Ten grades. Higher grades mean lower weakness values and therefore lower likelihood.

scale_ends_source.top: All controls adequate, appropriate and effective
